##Problem 1

```{r load}
library(tidyverse)

library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")

glimpse(ny_noaa)
```
```{r data-summary}
#To view the number of weather stasions & date rage
station_summary = ny_noaa %>%
  summarise(
    n_stations = n_distinct(id),
    first_date = min(date, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_date = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

print(station_summary)

missing_summary = ny_noaa %>%
  summarise(
    #view the number of the missing value in every column
    across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))
  ) %>%
  #Change the data missing-value table form horizonal to vertical
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_n"
  ) %>%
  #Calculate the missing percentage for each variable
  mutate(
    missing_percent = 100 * missing_n / nrow(ny_noaa)
  )

missing_summary

```
The NY NOAA dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables from 747 weather stations in New York State, covering from January 1, 1981, through December 31, 2010. Each row represents a daily weather record for one station. The variables include station ID (`id`), observation date(`date`), precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`).

There are no missing values in `id` or `date`. However, 5.62% of precipitation values, 14.69% of snowfall values, and 22.80% of snow depth values are missing. Both maximum and minimum temperature have about 43.71% missing values. Missing data are therefore a substantial issue, like for temperature analyses. And it could affect comparisons across stations and years if missingness varies between these groups.

```{r cleaning}
#Cleaning data
noaa_clean = ny_noaa %>%
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax)/10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)/10,
    prcp = prcp/10
  )

glimpse(noaa_clean)
summary(
  select(noaa_clean, tmax, tmin, prcp, snow, snwd)
)

```
```{r snowfall}
snowfall_counts = noaa_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(snow)) %>%
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

snowfall_counts
```
The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm. Because many days have no snowfall.


```{r monthly-temperature, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#Average maximum temperatures in January and July
monthly_temp = noaa_clean %>%
  filter(
    month %in% c(1, 7),
    !is.na(tmax)
  ) %>%
  group_by(id, year, month) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax),
    n_days = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

ggplot(
  monthly_temp,
  aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15, color = "blue", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "blue", size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ month, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Average daily maximum temperature by station and year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

July is much warmer than January, and January shows larger changes across years. Many stations follow similar patterns, with some years being warmer or colder than others. For example, January 2003 looks especially cold.

There are also a few possible outliers. One station has an unusually low July average of about 14°C around 1988.
